en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.1 (Tapokammasutta) The First Chapter: On Ascetic Practices At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these three kinds of ascetic practices. What three? The ascetic practice of mortification, the ascetic practice of self-mortification, and the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification. These, monks, are the three kinds of ascetic practices. “Monks, what is the ascetic practice of mortification? Here, monks, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept food brought or food specially prepared; he does not enter a house or sit down in a house; he does not eat from a vessel, or from the same dish as a woman or a man or a eunuch; he eats standing up, he eats only from the hand; he eats whatever is given, he eats only one kind of food; he lives on rice-husks, on rice-scum, on water, on ground flour, on forest roots and fruits, on fallen fruits, or he subsists by gleaning ears of grain; he wears coarse hempen cloth, cloth from a rubbish heap, a garment of bark-fiber, an antelope hide, a strip of antelope hide, a covering of kusa-grass, a blanket of wood-shavings, a cloak of head-hair, a cloak of animal-wool, a garment of owl’s wings; he is one who plucks out hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out hair and beard; he is one who stands continuously, refusing seats; he is one who squats continuously, devoted to the practice of squatting; he is one who uses a mattress of spikes; he makes a mattress of spikes his bed; he dwells pursuing the practice of bathing in water three times daily including the evening; thus in such a variety of ways he dwells pursuing the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body. This is called the ascetic practice of mortification. “And what, monks, is the ascetic practice of self-mortification? Here, monks, a certain person goes to the Himalayas, the abode of Rishis, where wild animals roam and where the cry of ‘hum’ resounds, and there he lives feeding on roots and fruits of the forest, dwelling at the foot of a tree, making the open air his shelter, using a cemetery, a forest grove, the foot of a tree, or a straw mat as his dwelling; he is one who accepts whatever seat is offered; he is one who never lies down, being devoted to sitting upright; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of wearing clothes made of cast-off rags; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living in the open air; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of not entering a village; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of not entering a village even for alms; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living in a remote forest; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living at the root of a tree; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living in a cemetery; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living in a jungle-thicket; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living in an open, unsheltered place; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of living wherever he happens to be; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of eating only what is collected; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of eating only one meal a day; he is one who dwells pursuing the practice of eating at every fourth meal-time, or at every sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, fourteenth, sixteenth, eighteenth, twentieth, twenty-fourth, twenty-sixth, twenty-eighth, thirtieth, thirty-second, thirty-fourth, or thirty-sixth meal-time, or he dwells pursuing the practice of eating once in seven days, or even once in half a month, subsisting by means of lumps of boiled rice collected from families. Thus in such a variety of ways he dwells pursuing the practice of mortifying and tormenting himself. This is called the ascetic practice of self-mortification. “And what, monks, is the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells restrained with the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of the restraint of the sense faculties, and possessed of restraint regarding livelihood. He dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification. “Of these three ascetic practices, monks, the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said: “Friend Ānanda, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Of these three ascetic practices, monks, the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Now, friend, how is the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent?

“Friend, the ascetic practice that is neither mortification nor self-mortification is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent because it leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Elated, that bhikkhu rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda. This is what was said by the Venerable Ānanda, and the Teacher confirmed it, saying, “So it is, Ānanda,” and the bhikkhus were satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda. Thus was this discourse spoken by the Venerable Ānanda while the Teacher was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, concerning the ascetic practices. And so it was with reference to this that this was spoken by the Blessed One. Therefore, it was designated as the Discourse on Ascetic Practices. Thus was this discourse spoken by the Blessed One, spoken by the Arahant, so I have heard. [End of] Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.1: The Discourse on Ascetic Practices. The First Chapter is finished. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“I am truly freed from that practice of self-mortification!
It is well that I am freed from that useless practice of self-mortification!
It is well indeed that I am freed and have attained enlightenment!”
Then Māra the Evil One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Those young brahmins who do not attain purity by departing from ascetic practices—”
“Though impure, you imagine yourself pure;
you have strayed from the path to purity.
Then the Blessed One, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” addressed Māra the Evil One in verses:
“Knowing that any asceticism which is not connected with the goal is not immortal,
all such things lead to ruin.”
Like a fletcher straightening a reed,
cultivate virtue, concentration, and wisdom—
the path to enlightenment.
“I have attained supreme purity;
you are defeated, O Ender!
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being miserable and dejected, vanished right there.

Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Now at that time, during the pitch-black darkness of night, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air while a fine rain was falling drop by drop.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in the Blessed One, manifested himself in the form of a great king of elephants and approached the Blessed One.
His head was like a great, precious *ariṭṭhaka* gem.
Just as if it were pure silver,
so are his teeth;
just as if it were a large plowshare.
Thus he became lustful.
Then the Blessed One, knowing, "This is Māra the Evil One," addressed Māra the Evil One with a verse:
"Wandering through the long course of saṃsāra..."
Having fashioned beauty and ugliness—
enough of that for you, O Evil One!
You are slain, O Ender!”
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, "The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me," being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the pitch-black darkness of night, while a single drop of rain fell.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he manifested various high and low forms of radiance not far from the Blessed One.
"Both the beautiful and the ugly.
Then the Blessed One, knowing "This is Māra the Evil One," addressed Māra the Evil One with verses:
"Wandering through the long course of saṃsāra..."
Having fashioned beautiful and ugly forms—
enough of that for you, O Evil One!
You are defeated, O Ender.
But those who are well-restrained in body, speech, and mind,
they do not follow the power of Māra.
“They are not bound by Māra. Then Māra... [as before] ...vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 4.4 (SN 4.4, SN 140, PTS [1st ed. SN i 105; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 234).
1. First Chapter: The First Discourse on Māra’s Snare.
Thus have I heard—
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“It was through wise attention and wise right effort, bhikkhus, that I attained supreme liberation; supreme liberation was realized by me.”
“Monks, by means of wise attention and wise right effort, you too shall attain unsurpassed liberation; you shall realize unsurpassed liberation.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“You are bound by the snare of Māra!”
“Whether they be divine or human,
you are bound by the fetters of Māra;
you shall not escape me, ascetic!”
“I am released from the snare of Māra,
both those that are divine and those that are human;
I am freed from the bondage of Māra.”
“You are slain, O End-maker!
Then Māra the Evil One... [as before] ...vanished right there.

1. First Chapter: The Second Discourse on the Snare of Māra.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"Monks, I am released from all snares, both those that are divine and those that are human.
You too, monks, are released from all snares, both those that are divine and those that are human."
"Go forth, bhikkhus, on tour for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.
Let not two of you go by one way.
Teach, bhikkhus, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; proclaim the holy life, entirely complete and pure."
“There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are falling away.
There will be those who understand the Dhamma.
And I too, monks, shall go to Uruvelā, to the village of Senāni, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.”
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“You are bound by all snares, both those that are divine and those that are human.”
“You are bound by great fetters;
you shall not escape me, ascetic.
“I am released from all snares.”
Whether they be divine or human,
I am liberated from the great bond;
you, O End-maker, are slain.
Then Māra the Evil One... [as before] ...vanished right there.

The Snake Discourse.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air during the pitch-black darkness of night, while a single drop of rain was falling.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in the Blessed One, manifested himself in the form of a great king of serpents and approached the Blessed One.
He was just like a large boat made from a single tree trunk.
Such was his body.
Just like a large fermenting vat, such was his hood.
Just as a large bronze bowl from Kosala,
so would his eyes be. Just as streaks of lightning flash when the sky is rumbling with thunder, so would they be.
Thus his tongue protrudes from his mouth.
Just as there is a sound from a smith’s bellows when they are being blown,
so too there is the sound of his inhalations and exhalations.
Then the Blessed One, knowing "This is Māra the Evil One," addressed Māra the Evil One in verses:
"The sage who frequents empty houses is truly well-restrained in himself."
He should cast it off and move on from there;
for that is what is appropriate for one such as he.
Many are the wanderers, and many are the fearsome things.
Moreover, though there be many gadflies and creeping things,
the Great Sage who has gone to an empty dwelling does not stir even a single hair.
The sky might split, the earth might shake,
and all living beings might tremble with fear;
even if they were to drive a stake into one's chest, [one would remain unshaken].
“The Buddhas do not seek refuge in acquisitions.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” pained and dejected, vanished right there.

1. First Chapter: The Discourse to Supati.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then the Blessed One, having walked back and forth in the open air for much of the night, washed his feet at the time of dawn and entered the dwelling.
He lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Why do you sleep? Why indeed do you sleep?
Why do you sleep like one who is unfortunate?
You sleep because the house is empty.”
"Why do you sleep now that the sun has risen?
"He for whom there is no ensnaring,
clinging craving to lead him anywhere— "
“With the total destruction of all acquisitions, the Buddha shall sleep;
what business have you here, Māra?
Then Māra the Evil One... [as before] ...vanished right there.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.8 (SN 4.8, SN 144, PTS [1st ed. SN i 107, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 240) 1. First Chapter: Nandati Sutta (The Discourse on Delighting) “Bhikkhus, when one delights in the eye, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. When one does not delight in the eye, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. When one delights in the ear… When one delights in the nose… When one delights in the tongue… When one delights in the body… When one delights in the mind, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. When one does not delight in the mind, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not arise. Seeing this danger in delighting, bhikkhus, the Noble Disciple here becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“One who has sons rejoices in his sons;
likewise, one who has cattle rejoices in his cattle.
A man’s rejoicing comes from acquisitions.”
"For he who is free from acquisitions does not rejoice.
"One with sons grieves because of his sons;
likewise, one with cattle grieves because of his cattle."
“From acquisitions comes a man’s sorrow;
he who is without acquisitions does not grieve.
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.9 First Chapter: The First Discourse on Life Span At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, life span is short; one must quickly do what is beneficial. There is no bargaining for the time of death. One should practice the holy life with the thought: ‘Perhaps I shall not die tonight. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, should one understand in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief by the Blessed One? “Bhikkhu, suppose there were a cloth that was clean and bright, free from dark spots, and it were placed upon a dyer’s stand. When the dyer applied the dye, it would take the dye well, become thoroughly saturated, and be perfectly prepared. So too, bhikkhu, when a bhikkhu possesses four qualities, he takes the training well, becomes thoroughly saturated with it, and is perfectly prepared. What four? Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is virtuous; possessing the Pātimokkha restraints, he dwells restrained by the restraints, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, and has stored up what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. He is an investigator of the Dhamma; he investigates the meaning of those teachings that have been learned by heart, examines them with his mind, and penetrates them well through right view. Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu takes the training well, becomes thoroughly saturated with it, and is perfectly prepared. It is in such a way, bhikkhu, that you should understand in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by me. The Rock Discourse.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, during the pitch-black darkness of night, the Blessed One was sitting out in the open air while a light rain was falling drop by drop.

Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horror of the hair standing on end in the Blessed One, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he shattered great boulders not far from the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, knowing "This is Māra the Evil One," addressed Māra the Evil One in verse:
"Even if all this were entirely..."
You may even shake Vulture Peak,
but for the Buddhas who are rightly liberated, there is no wavering.”
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being distressed and dejected, vanished right there.

The Kinnusīhasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly.
Then it occurred to Māra the Evil One:
“This ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a great assembly.
Suppose I were to approach the ascetic Gotama in order to cause him to lose his sight.”
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Why indeed do you roar like a lion, confident in the assembly? ... [The rest of the verse follows] ...”
"For you have a rival;
do you consider yourself a victor?
"The great heroes indeed roar," [he replied].
Confident in assemblies,
the Tathāgatas have attained power and have crossed over the attachment to the world.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

The Sakalikasutta.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park.
Now at that time, the Blessed One’s foot had been wounded by a splinter,
and intense bodily feelings were occurring for the Blessed One— painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, and unpleasant.
Yet the Blessed One endured them mindfully and clearly comprehending, without being disturbed.
Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Are you sleeping out of indolence, or are you merely intoxicated by poetry?”
"Are your needs not abundant? Are they not present?
Why then, being alone in a secluded lodging, do you lie here as if overcome by sleep?"
“I do not lie down out of sloth, nor am I intoxicated by poetry;
having realized the true goal, I am free from sorrow,
lying alone in a secluded dwelling.”
May I be compassionate toward all beings,
even those into whose chest an arrow has entered,
piercing their hearts again and again.
In this world, those who possess a dart find sleep;
therefore, being free from the dart, I do not sleep.
Waking, I neither dread nor fear sleeping.
Day and night they do not cause me remorse;
I see no decline anywhere in the world.
Therefore, I sleep well, being compassionate toward all beings.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, "The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me," being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

"Do not be attached to favor or opposition while practicing that way.

When he instructs others,

Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Pañcasālā, a brahmin village.
Now at that time, there were guests for the young maidens in Pañcasālā, the brahmin village.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms.
Now at that time, the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā were possessed by Māra the Evil One, thinking:
"May the ascetic Gotama not obtain any alms."
Then the Blessed One entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms with his bowl as clean as it had been washed, and he returned with his bowl as clean as it had been washed.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Did you obtain any alms, ascetic?"
“Indeed, Evil One, you have acted in such a way that I might not receive alms.
“In that case, Bhante, let the Blessed One enter Pañcasālā, the brahmin village, for alms a second time as well.
I shall act in such a way that the Blessed One will receive alms.”
“Māra has produced demerit by attacking the Tathāgata;
what do you think, O Evil One?”
Evil does not ripen for me.
Truly we live in great happiness,
we who possess nothing at all.
“We shall subsist on rapture, like the Ābhassara devas.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Second Chapter: The Discourse to the Farmers (Kassakasutta)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now on that occasion the Blessed One was instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk concerning Nibbāna.
And those bhikkhus listened to the Dhamma, paying close attention, applying their minds, focusing their whole hearts, and lending an attentive ear.
Then it occurred to Māra the Evil One:
"This ascetic Gotama is [engaged] with the monks in a Dhamma talk connected with Nibbāna...
What if I were to approach the ascetic Gotama in order to blind him?"
Then Māra the Evil One, having assumed the form of a farmer, with a large plough on his shoulder and holding a long goading stick, with disheveled hair and dressed in a hempen garment,
approached the Blessed One with feet smeared with mud; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Did you see the oxen, ascetic?
“But what have you to do with oxen, Evil One?
“The eye is mine, ascetic; forms are mine; the sphere of visual consciousness is mine.”
"Where can you go, ascetic, to escape from me?
The ear is mine alone, ascetic, and sounds are mine...
the nose is mine alone, ascetic, and odors are mine."
"Monk, the tongue is mine, tastes are mine;
monk, the body is mine, tangibles are mine;
monk, the mind is mine, mental phenomena are mine, and the sphere of mind-consciousness-contact is mine."
“Where, ascetic, will you go and be released?
“Even these, Evil One, are yours: your eye, your forms, and your sphere of visual-contact-consciousness.
But where, Evil One, there is no eye, no forms, and no sphere of visual-contact-consciousness—there, Evil One, is your range not found.”
The ear is yours alone, Evil One; sounds are yours; the sphere of auditory contact-consciousness is yours.
But where, Evil One, there is no ear, no sounds, and no sphere of auditory contact-consciousness, there is no range for you, Evil One.
The nose is yours alone, Evil One; odors are yours; the sphere of olfactory contact-consciousness is yours.
But where, Evil One, there is no nose, no odors, and no sphere of nose-contact consciousness, there is no range for you, Evil One.
Your own is the tongue, Evil One; your own are tastes, and your own is the sphere of tongue-contact consciousness...
[and so on] ...Your own is the body, Evil One; your own are tangibles, and your own is the sphere of body-contact consciousness... [and so on].
“Māra, your mind is yours; your mental objects are yours; your sphere of mind-contact and consciousness is yours.
But where, Māra, there is no mind, no mental objects, and no sphere of mind-contact and consciousness—there is no domain for you, O Evil One.
“That which they call ‘my mind’...”
And those who say "this is mine"— if your mind is set on these things,
O ascetic, you shall not escape from me.
“What they say is not mine;
those who say it am not I.
Know this, O Evil One:”
“You shall not see even my path.
Then Māra the Evil One... [as above] ...vanished right there.

2. The Second Chapter:
On Kingship (Rajjasutta).
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in a forest hut in the region of the Himalayas.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Is it possible to exercise sovereignty by means of Dhamma—without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without grieving or causing to grieve?
Then Māra the Evil One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One's mind, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One exercise sovereignty; let the Sugata exercise sovereignty—without killing, without causing to kill, without conquering, without causing to conquer, without grieving, without causing to grieve, and in accordance with the Dhamma.
“But what do you see in me, Evil One, that you speak to me thus:

‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One exercise sovereignty; let the Sugata exercise sovereignty—without killing, without causing to kill, without conquering, without causing to conquer, without grieving, without causing to grieve, and in accordance with the Dhamma’?”
“Venerable sir, the four bases for spiritual power have been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken by the Blessed One.
If the Blessed One so desired, venerable sir, he could resolve that the Himalayas, the king of mountains, be gold, and it would become gold. [The Blessed One said:
“As for the mountain being gold...”
Gold is entirely for oneself;
even two are not enough for one—
knowing this, one should live in harmony.
How could that person who has seen suffering and its source bow down to sensual pleasures?
Having understood that acquisition is a snare in the world, [how could they cling to it]?
“One should train for the sake of taming that very person.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
This is the second chapter.
Its summary verse:
The stone, the lion, the fragment,
the likeness, and the mind.
The bowl, the sense-base, the alms-food, the farmer, and the kingdom—these ten are yours.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 4.21 (SN 4.21, SN 157, PTS [1st ed. SN i 117; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 259)
3. Third Chapter:
Sambahula Sutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Silāvatī.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were dwelling not far from the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Then Māra the Evil One, having assumed the form of a brahmin and clothed in a great matted hair-tuft and a deerskin garment, [approached them].
Worn out, bent like a rafter, and gasping with a wheezing breath, he took a staff of *udumbara* wood and approached those bhikkhus.
Having approached them, he said this to those bhikkhus:
"Sirs, you are young renunciants—handsome, black-haired, endowed with auspicious youth, and in the prime of life, having not yet dallied with sensual pleasures."
“Enjoy, sirs, human sensual pleasures.
Do not abandon what is visible in this life to pursue what is temporal.
“But, brahmin, we do not abandon what is visible in this life to pursue what is temporal.”
“But, brahmin, we have abandoned what is subject to time and pursue what is visible in this very life.
For the Blessed One has said, brahmin, that sensual pleasures are subject to time, fraught with much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
This Dhamma, however, is visible in this very life, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.”
When this was said, Māra the Evil One shook his head, lashed out his tongue, raised a three-pronged crest on his forehead, leaned on his staff, and departed.
Then those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, we were dwelling not far from the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute."
Then, venerable sir, a certain brahmin— wearing a large mass of matted hair,
clad in a deerskin, old, hunchbacked like a roof-rafter, and gasping with a wheezing sound— approached us while carrying a staff of udumbara wood;
having approached, he said this to us:
"You are young, sirs, who have gone forth—young with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, and not yet having dallied with sensual pleasures.
Enjoy, sirs, human sensual pleasures!
Do not abandon what is visible and pursue what is temporal."
When this was said, venerable sir, we said this to that brahmin:
“We do not, brahmin, abandon what is directly visible in order to pursue what is temporal.
Rather, brahmin, we abandon what is temporal in order to pursue what is directly visible.”
“Indeed, brahmin, the Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are dark, full of suffering, full of despair, and the danger here is even greater.
This Dhamma is visible in this very life, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.
When this was said, venerable sir, that brahmin shook his head, lolled his tongue, raised a three-pronged wrinkle on his forehead, and leaning on his staff, he departed.
“Monks, this is not a brahmin.
This is Māra the Evil One, who has come here to confound you.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the significance of this matter, on that occasion recited this verse:
“How could a person who has seen suffering and its source bow down to sensual pleasures?
Having understood that acquisition is a snare in the world, [one should not do so].”
“One should train for the sake of disciplining that very person.

Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Samiddhi Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Silāvatī.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Samiddhi was dwelling not far from the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Then, while the Venerable Samiddhi was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"It is indeed a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me,
that I have such a teacher as the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed a great fortune for me,
that I have gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed a great fortune for me!
“May I have fellow celibates who are virtuous and of good character.
Then Māra the Evil One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Venerable Samiddhi, approached the Venerable Samiddhi;
having approached, he stood not far from the Venerable Samiddhi, manifesting a great terror and dread.
He made such a sound that, it seemed, even the earth itself shook.

Then the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
"Just now, Bhante, I was dwelling not far from the Blessed One, heedful, ardent, and resolute."
"Venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
'It is indeed a gain for me, it is indeed a great fortune for me,
that I have such a teacher— an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.'"
It is a gain for me indeed, it is a great fortune for me indeed,
that I have gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is a gain for me indeed, it is a great fortune for me indeed!
“‘May I have fellow celibates who are virtuous and of good character.
For me, Bhante, not far away there arose a great, terrifying, and fearful sound, and it was as if the earth itself were quaking.
“It is not the earth that is quaking, Samiddhi.”
“This is Māra the Evil One, who has come to blind you.
Go, Samiddhi; dwell right there, heedful, ardent, and resolute.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Samiddhi replied to the Blessed One. He rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
A second time, the Venerable Samiddhi remained right there, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
A second time, while the Venerable Samiddhi had gone into seclusion and was dwelling in solitude...
[as before] ...a second time, Māra the Evil One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Venerable Samiddhi’s mind... [as before] ...
It was as if the earth itself were sinking.
Then the Venerable Samiddhi addressed Māra the Evil One in verse:
“Out of faith I have gone forth;”
From the home to the homeless life;
mindfulness and wisdom are mine, O Buddhas,
and my mind is well-concentrated.
“Make forms as you wish;
they will not afflict me.
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhu Samiddhi knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Godhika was dwelling on the Black Rock on the side of Mount Isigili.
Then the Venerable Godhika, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained temporary liberation of mind.
Then the Venerable Godhika fell away from that temporary liberation of mind.
A second time, the Venerable Godhika, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained temporary liberation of mind.
A second time, the Venerable Godhika fell away from that temporary liberation of mind.
A third time, the Venerable Godhika, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained temporary liberation of mind.
A third time, the Venerable Godhika fell away from that... [as before] ...he fell away.
For a fourth time, the Venerable Godhika, being diligent... [as before] ...attained liberation.
For a fourth time, the Venerable Godhika fell away from that... [as before] ...he fell away.
For a fifth time, the Venerable Godhika... [as before] ...attained the liberation of mind.
A fifth time, the Venerable … [as before] … fell away from that liberation.
A sixth time, while the Venerable Godhika dwelt diligent, ardent, and resolute, he attained temporary liberation of mind.
A sixth time, the Venerable Godhika fell away from that temporary liberation of mind.
And for a seventh time, while dwelling heedful, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Godhika attained temporary liberation of mind.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Godhika:
"Six times now I have fallen away from temporary liberation of mind."
“What if I were to take up the knife?

Then Māra the Evil One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Venerable Godhika, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verses:

Now at that time, the Venerable Godhika had taken up a blade.
Then the Blessed One, knowing, "This is Māra the Evil One," addressed Māra the Evil One with a verse:

“Having uprooted craving together with its root,

3. Tatiyavagga Sattavassānubandhasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree.
Now at that time Māra the Evil One had followed the Blessed One for seven years, seeking an opening, looking for an opening, but finding none.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Are you meditating in the forest because you are overcome by sorrow?
Or have you lost your wealth, or are you longing for it?
Or have you perhaps committed some offense in the village?”
“Why do you not make a witness among people?
Why does no one become a witness for you?
“I have completely uprooted the entire root of sorrow.”
I meditate without fault, free from sorrow;
having severed all craving for existence,
I meditate without taints, O kinsman of the heedless.
“Those who say ‘This is mine’ and those who say ‘This is I’—
if your mind is fixed upon these things, [you will not escape suffering].”
“O ascetic, you shall not escape me!
“What they say is not mine;
those who speak are not I.”
“Know this, O Evil One:
you shall not see even my path.
“If the path has been fully realized...”
“Which leads to security and the deathless;
go away by yourself, leave us alone—
why do you try to instruct others?”
“Those people who seek the further shore ask about the domain of ministers;
being questioned by them, I explain.”
“That which is true is without substrate.
“Venerable sir, suppose there were a lotus pond not far from a village or a town,
and in it there were a crab.”
Then, venerable sir, many boys or girls might come out from that village or town and approach that lotus pond;
having approached, they would pull that crab out of the water and place it on dry land.
"Whatever claw that crab, venerable sir, might stretch out, those boys or girls would surely cut it off, break it, and crush it with a stick or a stone.
For in this way, venerable sir, with all its claws cut off, broken, and crushed, that crab would be unable to descend into that lotus pond."
“In the same way, Bhante, whatever deceptive displays, maneuvers, or writhings there may be, they have all been cut off, broken, and shattered by the Blessed One.
I am incapable, Bhante, of approaching the Blessed One again with the hope of finding an opening.
Then Māra the Evil One recited these verses of despondency in the presence of the Blessed One:
“A crow flew around a stone that had the color of fat, thinking:
‘Perhaps we might find something soft here.’”
There might even be gratification there. But not finding gratification therein,
Vāyasettha, one should depart.
“Having seized upon Kakudha as our refuge, we have become disillusioned with the Gotamas.

3. Third Chapter: The Discourse on the Daughters of Māra.
Then Māra the Evil One, having recited these verses of provocation in the presence of the Blessed One, departed from that place.
Having departed, he sat cross-legged on the ground not far from the Blessed One, silent, ashamed, with shoulders drooping and head cast down, brooding, speechless, scratching the earth with a stick.
Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāgā, the daughters of Māra, approached Māra the Evil One; having approached, they addressed Māra the Evil One in verse:
“Why are you dejected, dear one?
For what man do you grieve?
We shall bind him with the snare of passion.”
“Like an elephant in the forest,
we shall bind him and bring him here;
he will come under your control.”
“The Arahant, the Sugata in the world,
cannot be led astray by passion;
he has transcended the realm of Māra.”
"Therefore, we grieve greatly.
Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāgā, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Let us serve at your feet, ascetic!"
But the Blessed One paid no attention, for he was liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Then Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, having stepped aside, reflected thus:
"The intentions of men are indeed diverse."
"What if we were now to manifest ourselves each as a hundred maidens?
Then Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, having manifested themselves each as a hundred maidens, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they said this to the Blessed One:
"O ascetic, let us serve you at your feet."
The Blessed One paid no mind to her, as one who is liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Then Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, having stepped aside to one side, reflected thus:
"The intentions of men are indeed diverse."
“Suppose we were each to manifest a hundred forms of unproduced beauty.
Then Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, having each manifested a hundred forms of unproduced beauty, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they said this to the Blessed One:
“May we serve at your feet, O ascetic!”
The Blessed One paid no attention to her, as one who is liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Then Taṇhā and the others thought:
“…What if we were each to conjure up a hundred sons, all of the same appearance at once?”
Then Taṇhā and the others, having each manifested a hundred forms of those who had given birth but once, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said this to the Blessed One:
“We would serve at your feet, ascetic.”
The Blessed One paid no heed to them, as he was liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*).
Then Taṇhā and the others thought:
“…What if we were each to conjure up a hundred forms of difficult birth?”
Then Taṇhā and [the others]... having manifested a hundred forms of difficult birth, approached the Blessed One...
just as one liberated through the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
"Then Taṇhā and [the others]... might conjure up a hundred women of middle age. Then Taṇhā and [the others]...
Having manifested a hundred women of middle age...
[and so on] ...he was liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
Then craving... [and so on] ...
"Let me manifest a hundred forms of a great woman.
Then, having manifested a hundred forms of a great woman through craving... [and so on] ...where the Blessed One was... [and so on].
He was liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, stepping aside to one side, said this:
"Is it true, as we have heard, that our father spoke thus?"
The Arhat, the Sugata in the world,
cannot be led astray by passion;
he has transcended the realm of Māra.
"Therefore, we grieve greatly.

For if we were to employ such a method against a recluse or a brahmin who is not free from lust, his heart might burst, warm blood might gush from his mouth, or he might fall into madness or mental derangement.
Or rather, like a green reed cut down, it would wither, dry up, and shrivel away.
"In this very way, he would wither away, shrivel up, and dry out.
Then Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Taṇhā, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Are you meditating in the forest because you are overcome by sorrow?
Or have you lost your wealth, or are you longing for it?
Or have you perhaps committed some offense in the village?”
"Why do you not make a witness among people?
Why does no one become a witness for you?
"The attainment of the goal and peace of heart..."
Having conquered the army of pleasant and agreeable forms,
meditating alone, I have awakened to bliss;
therefore, I do not seek the company of people.
“No one can become my witness.
Then Aratī, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“How does a bhikkhu here dwell much, so that no one becomes his witness?”
"Having crossed the five floods, he has crossed over the sixth here;
how did he meditate so much that perceptions of sensual desire,
being external, do not find him?"
With body tranquil and mind well-liberated,
unconditioned, mindful, and homeless;
having realized the Dhamma, he meditates without applied thought.
He is not agitated, he does not forget,
and he is not dull. A bhikkhu who frequently dwells thus has crossed over the five floods and has crossed the sixth here.
"Thus meditating repeatedly, sensual perceptions become external to him who has not found that [bliss].
Then Rāgā, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Having cut off craving, though wandering in groups and companies,
many indeed will surely practice with faith;
truly, this homeless one will lead a great multitude.”
“Having cut through [the bonds], he will lead them beyond the realm of King Māra.
“Indeed, the Great Heroes, the Tathāgatas, lead [beings] by means of the True Dharma.”
“For those who lead by the Dhamma,
what envy can there be for those who understand?
Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, approached Māra the Evil One.
Māra the Evil One saw the daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga—approaching from afar.
Having seen them, he addressed them in verses:
“Fools, with lotus stalks...”
You would batter a mountain;
you would dig into a hill with your claws;
you would chew iron with your teeth.
Having struck the rock with your heads,
you shall find a firm footing in the abyss;
having seized the stump with your chests—
“Become disillusioned, O Gotamas!
“Radiant they have come:
Craving, Discontent, and Passion.”
The Teacher dispelled them there,
like the wind blowing away scattered cotton.
The third chapter.
Its summary verse:
Sambahula and Samiddhi,
and Godhika for seven years.
"O Buddha, Teacher, this 'Fivefold Māra' has been taught by the Best One.
Thus ends the Māra Saṃyutta.
